Medical History

- Current health concerns and risk factors:  2–3 days of new shortness of breath with wheeze and cough, first noted during a run; now occurs with brisk walking. Minimal/no relief from salbutamol (blue inhaler) despite daily/prophylactic use. No sputum. Known asthma; last asthma attack 3–4 years ago; no prior hospitalizations; no prior oral steroids. Last asthma review ~2 years ago. Baseline peak flow when well reportedly ~380 L/min; no current reading. Atopy (hay fever) and possible eczema.  
- Relevant family medical history:  Brother with asthma; sister with eczema (atopy).  
- Medications (including OTC or shared medications):  Salbutamol (blue) inhaler PRN, currently using daily and prophylactically (dose/route/frequency not documented); Clenil (beclomethasone, “brown” preventer) twice daily (exact dose not documented; advised to increase to 4 puffs twice daily); Cetraben topical (dose/route/frequency not documented); Hydrocortisone topical (dose/route/frequency not documented).

Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Key findings: Known asthma with atopic background (hay fever; family atopy). Acute onset (2–3 days) of wheeze, cough, exertional dyspnea; poor response to salbutamol; using preventer twice daily; baseline peak flow when well ~380 L/min; no current objective measures; no sputum; no prior steroids or hospitalizations; last asthma review 2 years ago.  
- Differential diagnoses (consistent with DDx):  
  - Mild-to-moderate acute asthma exacerbation on background of persistent asthma (High likelihood): classic triad of wheeze/cough/dyspnea over days with increased reliever use and inadequate relief in an atopic asthmatic.  
  - Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction contributing to current symptoms (Moderate likelihood): symptoms began with running and recur with brisk walking, though persistence beyond exercise suggests broader loss of control.  
  - Allergic asthma flare (Moderate likelihood): history of hay fever and family atopy; no specific allergen identified.  
  - Viral trigger possible (Low–Moderate likelihood): acute onset with cough but no systemic symptoms reported.  
  - Potential suboptimal inhaler technique/adherence (Moderate likelihood): frequent SABA with poor relief and medication confusion noted.  
- Working diagnosis: Acute asthma exacerbation (likely mild–moderate) on background of persistent asthma, with possible exercise/allergic triggers and potential inhaler technique issues.  
- Management priorities: Short-term step-up of inhaled corticosteroid, safe reliever use with clear safety-netting, prompt in-person review for examination and peak flow, and consideration of systemic therapy per findings.

Management Plan

- Actions and recommendations provided:  
  - Increase Clenil (beclomethasone “brown” inhaler) to 4 puffs twice daily while awaiting review.  
  - Use salbutamol (blue) inhaler as needed; up to every 2–4 hours. If requiring very frequent use or symptoms worsen, seek urgent care (ED/A&E).  
  - Schedule face-to-face GP appointment in the next few days for chest examination and peak flow measurement.  
  - Depending on examination/peak flow, may require oral steroids and/or antibiotics (per clinician discussion).  
- Follow-up: Patient advised to book an in-person review; attend ED/A&E urgently if breathing worsens before the appointment.  
- Patient education: Safety-net advice provided regarding increasing symptoms and high reliever use.

- Allied health referral (EPC – 10 visits):  Not recorded.

- Mental health support if indicated (e.g., psychologist, AMS support):  Not recorded.  
- CTG registration:  Not recorded.  
- Preventive health follow-up booked (e.g., flu vaccine, Pap test):  Advised to book face-to-face GP review; preventive items not recorded.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

- Acute asthma exacerbation (High): Wheeze, cough, exertional dyspnea over 2–3 days in known asthmatic; frequent SABA with poor relief.  
- Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (Moderate): Symptoms triggered by running and brisk walking; common in asthmatics.  
- Allergic asthma flare (Moderate): Atopic history (hay fever; family atopy) suggests possible allergen-related worsening.

Quality checks

- Missing but clinically expected elements: Smoking status; alcohol/substance use; full medication list with doses and devices (including spacer use); current peak flow and SpO2; vital signs (BP, pulse, respiratory rate); height/weight/BMI; inhaler technique assessment; immunization review (influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal as applicable); mental health screening; dietary assessment; cervical screening status; STI screening as indicated.  
- Internal contradictions between transcript and DDx: None significant. Minor medication naming confusion in transcript (initial mention of “Flanel/Bactroban” later clarified to Cetraben and hydrocortisone).  
- Transcript quality: Some speech was unclear/incomplete (telehealth), with fragmented phrases and potential transcription errors; objective measurements not obtained.
